q: What is circuit vision?
a: Using computer vision to turn a photo or drawing of a circuit (schematic or PCB) into structured data: detected components, connections, a netlist, or SPICE input.

q: Where should I start learning circuit vision?
a: Start with JKc66/CircuitVision (upload an image, see detected parts and a netlist), then study Image2schematic for the full pipeline, then the PCB detection repos, and Netlistify for SPICE-quality output.

q: What does JKc66/CircuitVision do?
a: It is a Streamlit app: you upload a circuit image, it detects components and builds a netlist. Good for a quick hands-on demo. Check its README for install steps.

q: What is Netlistify?
a: A research project from NYCU AI-EDA that converts schematic images into netlists/SPICE. Use it when you need simulation-oriented output. See the repo README for models and setup.

q: What is Image2schematic?
a: A project that goes from a PCB photo toward a schematic, showing the steps: preprocessing, component detection, and trace/connection reconstruction.

q: Which repo detects components on a PCB photo?
a: Look at s39674/PCB-Component-Detection and SanderGi/PCB-Detection. Try both on your own board photos and compare.

q: Schematic image vs PCB photo — what's the difference for CV?
a: A schematic is a clean line drawing of symbols and wires, so symbol detection plus line tracing works well. A PCB photo has real parts, shadows, traces on several layers, and hidden vias, so it is much harder and often incomplete.

q: What is a netlist?
a: A text list of the components and the nets (electrical nodes) that each pin connects to. It is what simulators and layout tools consume.

q: What is SPICE?
a: SPICE is a circuit simulator family. You feed it a netlist with component values and models, and it computes voltages and currents (DC, AC, transient). ngspice is a free open-source version.

q: How do I simulate a netlist?
a: Install ngspice, save the netlist as a .cir/.sp file with an analysis line (e.g. .tran or .op) and .end, then run: ngspice file.cir. See the ngspice manual for analysis commands.

q: What does a SPICE resistor line look like?
a: Format: R<name> <node1> <node2> <value>, e.g. R1 in out 10k. Capacitors start with C, inductors with L, diodes with D, voltage sources with V.

q: What is node 0 in SPICE?
a: Node 0 is ground, the reference for every voltage. Every SPICE circuit needs a path to node 0.

q: What is a .model statement?
a: It defines parameters for semiconductor devices (diodes, transistors), e.g. .model D1N4148 D(...). Without a correct model, simulation of active parts is not meaningful.

q: What is a BOM?
a: Bill of Materials: the list of part types, values, packages, and quantities. Detected components can be grouped into a BOM after CV.

q: What are reference designators?
a: Labels like R1, C3, U2, Q1, D4. The letter tells the part type: R resistor, C capacitor, L inductor, D diode, Q transistor, U IC, J connector, Y crystal, F fuse.

q: How do I identify a resistor?
a: Through-hole resistors are small cylinders with color bands; SMD resistors are small black rectangles with a printed number code (e.g. 103 = 10k). Schematic symbol: zigzag or rectangle. Designator R.

q: How do I read SMD resistor codes?
a: Three-digit code: two digits then the multiplier power of ten. 103 = 10 x 10^3 = 10 kΩ; 472 = 4.7 kΩ. An R marks the decimal point (4R7 = 4.7 Ω).

q: How do I identify a capacitor?
a: Ceramic SMD caps are tan/brown rectangles usually with no marking; electrolytics are cylinders with a stripe marking the negative lead. Symbol: two parallel plates (one curved for polarized). Designator C.

q: How do I tell diode polarity?
a: The band/stripe marks the cathode. In the symbol, the bar is the cathode and the triangle points toward it (direction of conventional current).

q: How do I identify an IC?
a: ICs are black packages with many pins (SOIC, QFP, QFN, BGA). A dot or notch marks pin 1. Designator U. Read the part number on top and look up the datasheet.

q: How do I find pin 1 on a chip?
a: Look for a dot, dimple, notch, or beveled edge; pin 1 is next to it, and pins count counter-clockwise from the top view on most packages.

q: How do I identify an inductor?
a: Often a coil of wire, or a block marked with a code; power inductors are larger dark squares. Symbol: a series of loops. Designator L.

q: How do I identify a transistor?
a: Three-terminal parts in TO-92, SOT-23, or TO-220 packages. Designator Q. Check the printed code against the datasheet to know the pinout.

q: How should I photograph a board for circuit vision?
a: Use even diffuse lighting, keep the camera parallel to the board, fill the frame, focus on markings, shoot both sides, and keep original full-resolution files. See the Photo checklist on the Circuit Vision page.

q: Why is glare a problem in PCB photos?
a: Glare washes out markings and makes shiny solder look like other features, which hurts detection and OCR. Use diffuse light or a polarizer and avoid direct flash.

q: What resolution should board photos be?
a: Use the highest resolution you can and avoid compression. Small SMD markings need many pixels; tile and stitch large boards rather than shrinking them.

q: What is YOLO?
a: YOLO is a fast object detection model family. In circuit vision it locates components with bounding boxes. Ultralytics documents training on custom datasets.

q: How do I train YOLO on my own components?
a: Label images with boxes per class (resistor, capacitor, ...), arrange them in YOLO format with a data YAML, then train with the Ultralytics CLI or Python API. Follow the Ultralytics training guide.

q: How many images do I need to train a detector?
a: There's no fixed number; more varied labeled images help. Start with a pretrained model and fine-tune; check validation mAP to see if you need more data.

q: What is mAP?
a: Mean Average Precision: the standard detection accuracy metric combining precision and recall across classes and IoU thresholds. Higher is better.

q: What is SAM (Segment Anything)?
a: Meta's Segment Anything Model produces pixel masks for objects from prompts like points or boxes. It can outline parts or traces, but it does not know component classes by itself.

q: Detection vs segmentation — which do I need?
a: Detection gives boxes + labels (good for counting/identifying parts). Segmentation gives exact pixel outlines (good for traces, pads, precise shapes). Many pipelines combine both.

q: How do I read part markings with OCR?
a: Crop each detected component and run OCR (e.g. EasyOCR) on it. Tiny laser-etched text often needs upscaling, contrast enhancement, and manual checking.

q: Why does OCR fail on chip markings?
a: Markings are small, low-contrast, and often rotated. Improve lighting, crop tightly, rotate upright, upscale, and verify manually.

q: How are wires/connections found in a schematic image?
a: Pipelines remove detected symbols, then trace remaining lines (e.g. with thresholding and line/contour detection) and find junctions to group pins into nets.

q: Can circuit vision recover connections from a PCB photo?
a: Only partially. Top-layer traces are visible, but inner layers and vias under parts are hidden. Expect to verify with a multimeter continuity check or the design files.

q: How do I verify a CV-generated netlist?
a: Compare against the schematic or design files, spot-check nets with a continuity meter, check that every part has the expected pin count, and simulate a simple case.

q: Which tool should I use for a quick demo?
a: CircuitVision (Streamlit) is the fastest way to show image → parts → netlist.

q: Which tool for SPICE-ready output?
a: Netlistify targets schematic-to-netlist conversion for simulation.

q: How do I run a Streamlit app?
a: Install requirements (pip install -r requirements.txt), then run: streamlit run <app file>.py and open the local URL it prints. Check the repo README for the exact file name.

q: What is a Python virtual environment and why use one?
a: A venv isolates a project's packages: python -m venv .venv, then activate it and pip install. It avoids version conflicts between repos.

q: Do I need a GPU?
a: Inference on a few images works on CPU. Training detectors is much faster with an NVIDIA GPU; cloud notebooks are an option.

q: What is image preprocessing?
a: Steps like resizing, grayscale, denoising, contrast adjustment, thresholding, and perspective correction that make images easier for models.

q: How do I fix a tilted photo?
a: Apply a perspective transform (homography) using the four board corners, e.g. with OpenCV getPerspectiveTransform + warpPerspective.

q: What is a footprint vs symbol?
a: A symbol is the schematic drawing; a footprint is the physical copper pad pattern on the PCB. The same part has both.

q: What is a via?
a: A plated hole connecting copper layers. Vias hide connections between layers, which limits photo-based reconstruction.

q: What should I include in a CV handoff?
a: Original images, board name/revision, which side is which, the detected component list with confidence, open questions, and any manual corrections.

q: What is labeling/annotation for training?
a: Drawing boxes or masks on images and assigning class names so a model can learn. Consistent class definitions matter more than tools.

q: How do I measure if a model is good enough?
a: Hold out a test set of your real boards, check precision/recall per class, and review false detections visually.

q: What is a confidence threshold?
a: Detections below the threshold are discarded. Raise it for fewer false positives, lower it to miss fewer parts.

q: Where do I start learning network automation?
a: Begin with NetAutLabs for hands-on labs and CiscoDevNet/netprog_basics for fundamentals, then learn Netmiko, then labs-as-code with Containerlab or netlab.

q: What is SSH?
a: Secure Shell: encrypted remote CLI access, normally TCP port 22. It's the main way to log into network devices and what Netmiko uses.

q: How do I enable SSH on a Cisco IOS device?
k: enable ssh cisco ios crypto key
a: Typical steps: set hostname and ip domain-name, crypto key generate rsa (2048 bits), ip ssh version 2, create a local user, then on line vty 0 4 set transport input ssh and login local. Check your platform's guide.

q: Why can't I SSH to a device?
a: Check reachability (ping), that port 22 is open/ACLs allow you, SSH is enabled with keys generated, vty lines allow ssh, and credentials are correct. 'Connection refused' usually means SSH not enabled; timeout usually means path/firewall.

q: What is Netmiko?
a: A Python library by Kirk Byers that simplifies SSH to many network vendors: connect, send show commands, push config, save.

q: How do I install Netmiko?
a: pip install netmiko (ideally inside a virtual environment).

q: How do I run a show command with Netmiko?
a: Create ConnectHandler(**device) with device_type, host, username, password, then output = conn.send_command('show ip interface brief').

q: How do I push config with Netmiko?
a: Use conn.send_config_set([list of commands]); it enters and exits config mode for you. Then conn.save_config() if needed.

q: What device_type should I use in Netmiko?
a: It matches the platform, e.g. cisco_ios, cisco_nxos, cisco_xr, arista_eos, juniper_junos. The Netmiko docs/repo list supported platforms.

q: How do I get structured output from Netmiko?
a: Pass use_textfsm=True to send_command to parse output into Python data using TextFSM/ntc-templates when a template exists.

q: Netmiko times out — what do I do?
a: Increase read_timeout on send_command for slow commands, check the prompt is detected, and confirm the device_type is correct.

q: How do I keep passwords out of scripts?
a: Read them from environment variables, getpass, or a vault (e.g. Ansible Vault). Never commit them to Git.

q: What is a VLAN?
a: A Virtual LAN splits one switch into separate Layer 2 broadcast domains, identified by a VLAN ID (1-4094).

q: How do I create a VLAN on Cisco IOS?
a: conf t, vlan 10, name USERS, then on an access port: interface Gi0/1, switchport mode access, switchport access vlan 10.

q: What is a trunk port?
a: A link that carries multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags, typically between switches or to a router/firewall.

q: Access port vs trunk port?
a: An access port carries one untagged VLAN for an end device; a trunk carries several tagged VLANs between network devices.

q: Devices in the same VLAN can't talk — why?
k: vlan troubleshoot connectivity not working broken cannot talk ping fail
a: Check both ports are in the same VLAN, the VLAN exists, the trunk allows it, the ports are up, and IP addresses are in the same subnet.

q: What is routing?
a: Forwarding packets between different IP networks based on a routing table. Routes come from connected interfaces, static config, or dynamic protocols like OSPF and BGP.

q: How do I add a static route?
a: Cisco IOS: ip route <destination> <mask> <next-hop>, e.g. ip route 10.2.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.1.

q: What is a default route?
a: A route matching everything not otherwise known: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop>. Commonly points to the internet edge.

q: What is OSPF?
a: A link-state interior routing protocol: routers share link info within areas and compute shortest paths. Common in enterprise networks.

q: What is BGP?
a: Border Gateway Protocol exchanges routes between autonomous systems (internet, data centers). It's policy-driven and runs over TCP 179.

q: How do I check the routing table?
a: Cisco: show ip route. Look for the route to your destination and its next hop.

q: What is a subnet mask?
a: It splits an IP into network and host parts. /24 = 255.255.255.0 = 256 addresses (254 usable hosts).

q: How do I troubleshoot connectivity step by step?
a: Go bottom up: link/interface up? correct VLAN? IP/mask/gateway right? ping gateway, then destination; traceroute to see where it stops; check ACLs and routes.

q: What does show ip interface brief tell me?
a: Each interface's IP and its status/protocol. up/up is healthy; administratively down means shutdown is configured; up/down often means a Layer 2 problem.

q: What is NETCONF?
a: An IETF protocol (RFC 6241) to read/change config using XML RPCs, usually over SSH port 830. Supports candidate configs and commit on capable devices.

q: What is RESTCONF?
a: An HTTP-based protocol (RFC 8040) to access YANG-modeled data with GET/PUT/PATCH/POST/DELETE, using JSON or XML.

q: What is YANG?
a: A data modeling language describing device configuration and state. NETCONF and RESTCONF use YANG models.

q: NETCONF vs RESTCONF — which should I use?
a: NETCONF has richer transactions (candidate datastore, locking); RESTCONF is simpler for web/REST tooling. Use what your platform supports and your tools prefer.

q: NETCONF/RESTCONF vs CLI scraping?
a: APIs return structured data and validate changes; CLI scraping (Netmiko) works everywhere but needs output parsing. Many teams use both.

q: What is Ansible?
a: An agentless automation tool. You write YAML playbooks that run tasks against an inventory of hosts; for network devices it connects via SSH/APIs.

q: How do I configure Cisco devices with Ansible?
a: Use the cisco.ios collection (e.g. cisco.ios.ios_config, ios_vlans) with ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli and ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios.

q: What is an Ansible inventory?
a: A file listing hosts and groups (INI or YAML) plus variables like connection type and OS.

q: What is an Ansible role?
a: A reusable bundle of tasks, templates, variables, and handlers with a standard folder layout, so playbooks stay short.

q: How do I do a dry run in Ansible?
a: Run ansible-playbook with --check (and --diff to see changes). Not every module supports check mode.

q: What is Ansible Vault?
a: It encrypts sensitive variables/files: ansible-vault create secrets.yml; run playbooks with --ask-vault-pass.

q: What is Nornir?
a: A Python automation framework: inventory plus concurrent task execution, using plugins like Netmiko or NAPALM. It's Ansible-like but pure Python.

q: Nornir vs Ansible?
a: Ansible uses YAML playbooks and is easy to share; Nornir is Python code, faster and more flexible for developers. Pick based on your team's skills.

q: What is NAPALM?
a: A Python library with a vendor-neutral API for getting facts and replacing/merging config, with compare_config and rollback on supported drivers.

q: What is Containerlab?
a: A tool to build network labs from a YAML topology file using container-based network OSs. clab deploy -t file.clab.yml starts it.

q: How do I start a Containerlab topology?
a: sudo containerlab deploy -t mylab.clab.yml; inspect with containerlab inspect; remove with containerlab destroy -t mylab.clab.yml.

q: What is netlab?
a: A tool by ipSpace that builds labs from a high-level topology and also configures routing protocols for you, using Containerlab or libvirt as providers.

q: Containerlab vs netlab?
a: Containerlab deploys nodes and links; netlab sits on top, generating topology plus device configs (addressing, OSPF, BGP...). Use netlab for quick protocol labs.

q: What is topology-as-code?
a: Describing your lab in a version-controlled file (YAML) so it can be rebuilt identically any time. Containerlab and netlab do this.

q: Where can I practice on real Cisco gear for free?
a: Cisco DevNet Sandboxes and Learning Labs provide free lab environments.

q: How do I back up a device config?
a: Save show running-config to a dated file (Netmiko, Ansible, or a tool like Oxidized/RANCID), ideally committed to Git.

q: How do I roll back a bad change?
a: Options: re-apply the backup, use configure replace (Cisco IOS archive), commit confirmed / rollback on Junos/IOS-XR, or NAPALM rollback. Plan the rollback before the change.

q: What is commit confirmed?
a: On Junos/IOS-XR, a commit that rolls back automatically unless you confirm within a timer, protecting you from locking yourself out.

q: What should a change checklist include?
a: Approval/window, backup, pre-checks, the exact commands, lab test, post-checks, rollback plan, and ticket notes. See the Config change checklist on the Networks page.

q: Running-config vs startup-config?
a: running-config is live in memory; startup-config loads at boot. Save with copy running-config startup-config (or write memory) or changes are lost on reload.

q: How do I avoid locking myself out?
a: Use commit confirmed or 'reload in 10' before risky changes, keep console/out-of-band access, and apply ACLs carefully.

q: How do I store configs in Git?
a: Back up configs to a repo on a schedule, commit with timestamps, and use diffs to see what changed.

q: What is idempotency?
a: Running the same automation twice gives the same result without extra changes. Ansible resource modules aim for this.

q: What is Jinja2 templating?
a: A template language used to generate configs from variables, e.g. {{ hostname }}. Ansible and many Python tools use it.

q: What is TextFSM?
a: A template-based parser that turns CLI output into tables; ntc-templates provides many ready-made templates.

q: Where can I find more network automation tools?
a: The networktocode awesome-network-automation list collects tools, books, and communities.

q: What is SNMP?
a: Simple Network Management Protocol polls device counters/status and sends traps. Use SNMPv3 for authentication and encryption.

q: What is streaming telemetry / gNMI?
a: Devices push structured data continuously (often via gNMI over gRPC) instead of being polled, for faster monitoring.

q: What is an ACL?
a: An ordered list of permit/deny rules on packets. It ends with an implicit deny, so order and a final permit matter.

q: How do I test automation safely?
a: Run against a Containerlab/netlab copy or a DevNet sandbox first, use check/dry-run modes, then a small pilot group.

q: What is Python's role in network automation?
a: Python drives most libraries (Netmiko, NAPALM, Nornir). Learn basics: variables, lists/dicts, loops, functions, files, and JSON.

q: How do I call a REST API from Python?
a: Use the requests library: requests.get(url, auth=..., headers={'Accept':'application/yang-data+json'}, verify=...). Check status_code then .json().

q: What port does NETCONF use?
a: NETCONF over SSH uses TCP port 830 by default.
